title: Cline CLI npm Package Compromised via Suspected Cache Poisoning Attack

reading.body:
An AI system deployed to triage GitHub issues for the Cline open-source project was given excessive permissions, including access to publishing credentials for multiple package repositories. An attacker could inject prompts into issue titles to make the AI execute arbitrary commands and steal those credentials, potentially deploying malware to millions of users. The vulnerability existed for over two months because the system ran without human review of its actions.

This is a prompt injection attack on a deployed automation system. The AI model itself was not the failure; the failure was architectural, running unsupervised with high-privilege access to production secrets. A human approval step before credential use, or credential rotation policies, or limiting AI system permissions to read-only operations, would have prevented the attack from reaching users.

It is not established whether credentials were actually stolen or used to deploy malware during the vulnerability window.

summary:
# Summary

Cline, an open-source AI coding tool used by millions of developers, contained a critical security vulnerability from December 2025 to February 2026. The flaw existed in an AI-powered issue triage workflow that ran on the GitHub repository with excessive privileges. A researcher named Adnan Khan discovered that attackers could exploit a prompt injection vulnerability by creating issues with specially crafted titles that tricked the AI into executing malicious commands. This could potentially allow attackers to steal publishing credentials and deploy malware to the VS Code Marketplace, OpenVSX, and NPM package repository, affecting millions of users worldwide.

Khan disclosed the vulnerability through multiple channels starting January 1st but received no response from the Cline team for over a month. After public disclosure on February 9th, the team fixed the issue within one hour by removing the vulnerable workflow and revoking credentials. Evidence suggests someone may have attempted to exploit the vulnerability, though no malicious updates were released. Khan recommends users disable auto-updates for Cline until the team confirms no credentials were compromised during the vulnerability window.
